sec.title: Purpose
sec.p: Increased depression, anxiety and stress symptoms are associated with reduced mindfulness levels and coping skills. This study primarily aimed to investigate (1) the relationships between mindfulness, coping styles, depression, anxiety and stress and (2) mindfulness and coping styles as predictors of depression, anxiety and stress in adults who stutter. A secondary aim was to compare mindfulness, coping styles, depression, anxiety and stress levels in adults who stutter according to stuttering severity.

sec.title: Method
sec.p: This exploratory study included 47 adults who stutter who completed a full online survey in Turkish to gather demographic information, mindfulness, coping styles, depression, anxiety and stress scores. Participants were interviewed remotely to assess their stuttering severity. The correlation and hierarchical regression analysis were applied.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Significant positive relationships between depression and anxiety, depression and stress, and anxiety and stress scores were found. Mindfulness significantly explained 24.9% of the stress levels in adults who stutter, and helpless and submissive coping styles significantly explained 43.8% of the depression and 31.4% of the anxiety levels.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: This study showed a correlation between elevated stress, anxiety and depression levels. Frequent use of passive coping mechanisms and lower mindfulness scores were found to be predictors of depression, anxiety and stress in adults who stutter.

p.italic: What is already known on this subject

list-item.p: Stress, anxiety and depression are interrelated, with research revealing mixed findings regarding the relationship between stuttering and depression. However, stuttering is consistently associated with heightened anxiety levels, particularly state anxiety. Increased mindfulness has been linked to reduced stress, anxiety and depression, with studies indicating that individuals who stutter exhibit lower negative impacts of stuttering when mindfulness levels are higher. Additionally, coping strategies—whether active or passive—are associated with stress levels, with active coping correlating with more favorable outcomes. Research suggests that individuals who stutter and employ active coping mechanisms, such as seeking social support, manage stress more effectively.

p.italic: What this paper adds to the existing knowledge

list-item.p: This study contributes to the literature by confirming the significant relationships between depression, anxiety and stress in adults who stutter and highlighting mindfulness and passive coping styles as predictors of these variables. Specifically, lower mindfulness levels and more frequent use of passive coping strategies were associated with higher depression, anxiety and stress levels.

p.italic: What are the potential or actual clinical implications of this work?

list-item.p: These findings suggest that individuals who stutter may benefit from interventions targeting mindfulness and active coping strategies to better manage stress, anxiety and depression, with implications for clinical practice.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: People who stutter are at increased risk of experiencing stereotypes, prejudices and bullying, which can lead to negative thoughts, emotions and cognitive‐affective outcomes (Craig et al. 2009; Iverach et al. 2009; Menzies et al. 2009). Variability in stuttering severity, duration, and/or frequency over time has also been found to adversely affect adults who stutter (Tichenor and Yaruss 2021). A range of personal, environmental and social factors contribute to negative outcomes (e.g., Tichenor and Yaruss 2019), including elevated anxiety (e.g., Iverach et al. 2009; Kraaimaat et al. 2002; St Clare et al. 2009), internalized stigma (Boyle 2013) and reduced quality of life (Craig et al. 2009). However, not all people who stutter experience these adverse outcomes to the same degree, highlighting the important individual differences in psychological resilience and vulnerability. This variability suggests the presence of protective factors that may buffer against the impact of stuttering‐related challenges. Mindfulness has emerged as one such factor, given its associations with emotional regulation and reduced psychological distress. Research suggests that mindfulness facilitates adaptive responses to internal experiences—including negative thoughts and emotions—by increasing acceptance and reducing reactivity (e.g., Boyle 2011; Brown and Ryan 2003; Israel et al. 2023). Similarly, the use of active coping strategies—such as problem‐solving and cognitive restructuring—has been shown to be beneficial in managing stuttering‐related stress and mitigating its emotional consequences (e.g., Plexico et al. 2009a). Evidence suggests that individuals with higher mindfulness and more frequent use of active coping strategies report lower levels of stress, anxiety and depression (Kaya et al. 2007; Weinstein et al. 2009). These adaptive traits and behaviours may play a key role in promoting psychological well‐being by helping adults who stutter navigate complex social, emotional and communicative challenges. Despite these insights, the relationships between depression, anxiety, stress, mindfulness and coping styles in adults who stutter remain underexplored. The current study aims to examine the associations among these variables in adults who stutter.

sec.title: Depression, Anxiety and Stress
sec.p: Stress‐ and anxiety‐inducing events have been linked to an increased risk of depression (Mahmoud et al. 2012; Tennant 2002). Several studies examining depressive symptoms in adults who stutter have yielded inconsistent findings (Briley et al. 2021; Tran et al. 2011; Tudor et al. 2013). For example, Tran and colleagues (2011) found that adults who stutter exhibited higher depressive mood than 200 age‐ and sex‐matched peers, whereas Tudor and colleagues (2013), using the Beck Depression Inventory (BDI; Beck et al. 1996) with 21 adults who stutter and 21 matched peers, found no group differences in self‐reported depression scores. Given that anxiety‐inducing events increase the risk of depression and that anxiety is closely linked to stuttering (e.g., Iverach et al. 2009; Kraaimaat et al. 2002; St Clare et al. 2009), these inconsistent findings highlight the complex relationship between stuttering and depression.

Evidence indicates that adults who stutter tend to experience higher state anxiety than trait anxiety (Aydın Uysal and Ege 2020), and meta‐analytic findings further show significantly higher levels of trait and social anxiety levels in adults who stutter than their peers who do not stutter (Craig and Tran 2014). Iverach et al. (2009) found that adults who stutter had a six‐ to seven‐fold increased risk of meeting criteria for an anxiety disorder compared to age‐ and gender‐matched controls. Although anxiety does not directly cause stuttering, it may coexist with it or arise in response to personal, social, or environmental factors related to stuttering (i.e., Iverach et al. 2009; Iverach and Rapee 2014).

Stress has also been associated with stuttering (Plexico et al. 2005; Plexico et al. 2009a). For example, Plexico and colleagues (2009a) qualitatively explored coping experiences in 9 adults who stutter (7 male, 2 female), finding that most perceived stuttering as stressful prior to, during, and following moments of disfluency. Previous research indicates that adults with higher mindful awareness levels and more frequent use of active coping strategies tend to report lower stress, anxiety and depression scores (Kaya et al. 2007; Weinstein et al. 2009). Research has shown associations between lower stress, anxiety and depression levels and higher mindfulness or more frequent use of active coping strategies (Kaya et al. 2007; Muris et al. 2001; Palmer and Rodger 2009; Weinstein et al. 2009), which is indicative of these constructs warranting closer examination in adults who stutter.

sec.title: Mindfulness
sec.p: Mindfulness refers to present‐moment awareness characterized by non‐judgmental attention to ongoing experiences (Brown and Ryan 2003), which is conceptualized as a transient state or as a more stable trait (Baer 2003; Brown and Ryan 2003). Higher mindfulness scores have been associated with lower levels of perceived stress, reduced anxiety and less frequent use of passive coping strategies (Weinstein et al. 2009).

Research concerning mindfulness in adults who stutter has expanded in recent years (Beilby et al. 2012; Israel et al. 2023; Medina et al. 2023). For example, Israel and colleagues (2023) used an online survey to investigate the levels of mindfulness, self‐compassion, decentralization capacity and impact of stuttering with 150 adults who stutter. According to the authors, adults who stutter with higher trait mindfulness scores reported lower scores for the adverse impacts of stuttering. Medina and colleagues (2023) examined the results of an 8‐week remote mindfulness training with five adults who stutter and assessed their quality of life with the Overall Assessment of the Speaker's Experience of Stuttering (OASES; Yaruss and Quesal 2006). According to the authors, the OASES ratings of three participants were improved following the therapy. Beilby and colleagues (2012) assessed the mindfulness levels of 20 adults who stutter who participated in acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT), which has six core processes, one of which is mindfulness. The researchers reported increases in the Mindful Attention Awareness Scale (MAAS; Brown and Ryan 2003) and the Kentucky Inventory of Mindfulness Skills (KIMS; Baer 2003) scores. They interpreted the increase in MAAS scores as suggesting greater openness and receptivity to experiences in the present moment across cognitive, emotional, physical, interpersonal and general life domains. The increase in KIMS scores was interpreted as a higher tendency to be mindful on a regular basis through the acquisition of various mindfulness skills. These findings provide evidence that there is a link between increased mindfulness levels and decreased adverse impacts of stuttering; however, there is much that needs to be explored in this relationship.

sec.title: Coping Styles
sec.p: Coping refers to intentional efforts to manage stressful occurrences or situations (Compas et al. 2001). Coping styles have a significant impact on physiological well‐being (Farley et al. 2005). Various coping styles (Skinner et al. 2003) are often grouped into active or passive styles (Nielsen and Knardahl 2014). Active coping styles (e.g., seeking social support, positive reframing, problem‐solving) are typically adaptive, whereas passive strategies (e.g., avoidance, withdrawal, substance use) are generally maladaptive (Wood and Bhatnagar 2015). Coping strategies may vary depending on the situation or the person who uses them. In some cases, taking action may help to solve a perceived problem, while in others, regulating emotions and thoughts may be useful for active coping.

Few studies have investigated coping responses in adults who stutter (Plexico et al. 2009a, 2009b; Vanryckeghem et al. 2004). Vanryckeghem and colleagues (2004) investigated speech‐related coping responses with 46 adults who stutter and 76 adults who did not stutter using a self‐report questionnaire (i.e., the Behaviour Checklist; Brutten and Vanryckeghem 1974). The authors reported significantly greater differences in speech‐associated coping responses between adults who stutter and those who did not stutter in situations of disrupted speech and emphasized the need for further research in coping. Plexico and colleagues (2009a, 2009b) explored what adults who stutter do or think to cope with stuttering. The researchers applied grounded theory by conducting qualitative interviews and analysis with nine adults who stutter (M/F = 7/2). They reported a total of four core categories that play a key role in coping with stuttering and presented them in two companion papers. The first presented two core categories that play a key role in coping with stuttering: the listeners, who are the primary beneficiaries of coping efforts, and the degree of self‐acceptance of the speaker (Plexico et al. 2009a). The participants reported that when they perceived stuttering as a disturbing, misunderstood and uncontrollable characteristic for the listener and as a shameful characteristic that defined the individual's entire self‐concept, they tended to use passive coping strategies (i.e., avoidance or escape). In their second paper, the authors reported the other two core categories that play a key role in coping with stuttering: putting aside their concerns about listeners' reactions and trying to cope on their own behalf (Plexico et al. 2009b). The authors suggested that participants reported feeling more connected to listeners and used active coping techniques (i.e., approach coping) more frequently when they acknowledged that stuttering played a part in their lives but did not completely define who they were. In adults who stutter, coping responses appear closely tied to the perceived controllability and social meaning of stuttering events.

sec.title: The Present Study
sec.p: Overall, mounting evidence suggests that individuals with higher levels of mindfulness and more frequent use of active coping strategies tend to experience lower levels of stress, anxiety and depression (Kaya et al. 2007; Muris et al. 2001; Palmer and Rodger 2009; Weinstein et al. 2009). Investigating the relationships between mindfulness, coping styles, depression, anxiety and stress, as well as the effects of mindfulness and coping styles as predictors of these variables in adults who stutter, is expected to contribute to the knowledge of decision‐making processes for the management of stuttering in adults who stutter.

Prior research suggests that the adverse impacts of stuttering, which include personal, physiological and environmental factors (Tichenor and Yaruss 2019), do not have a strong correlation with behavioural measures of stuttering, such as stuttering frequency and severity (Blumgart et al. 2012; Manning and Gayle Beck 2013). Nonetheless, this study secondarily aimed to investigate if stuttering severity groups (very mild‐mild, moderate, severe‐very severe) varied in terms of depression, anxiety, stress, mindfulness and coping styles in order to contribute to the body of knowledge. Thus, this study primarily aimed to examine (1) the relationships among mindfulness, coping styles and levels of depression, anxiety and stress, and (2) the predictive roles of mindfulness and coping styles in explaining symptoms of depression, anxiety and stress, while secondarily aiming to compare these variables across adults who stutter with varying stuttering severity. In this context, this study sought to answer the following research questions:
What is the nature of the relationship between depression, anxiety and stress levels and the levels of mindfulness and stress coping styles in adults who stutter?
To what extent do mindfulness and stress coping styles predict the levels of depression, anxiety and stress among adults who stutter?
Are there significant differences in mindfulness, stress coping styles, and levels of depression, anxiety and stress across adults who stutter with varying stuttering severity?

sec.title: Research Design
sec.p: The data for this exploratory study were collected through remote interviewing and via web‐based forms administered remotely. The form that was delivered to the participants included demographic information, followed by surveys. Lokman Hekim University Ethics Committee granted ethical approval for this research (2022/11; No: 2022099).

sec.title: Participants and Recruitment
sec.p: Forty‐seven adults who stutter (age range = 18–68, mean = 31.25; 13 females and 37 males) participated in this study. The researchers publicized the study on social media (e.g., Instagram and WhatsApp groups), contacted stuttering organizations in Turkey (the association's website: https://kekemelerdernegi.com), and informed speech and language therapists about the study via the National Association of Speech and Language Therapists. Participants who volunteered to take part in the study contacted the researchers using the contact information provided. The participants were informed about the study and that they could leave it whenever they wanted.

sec.title: Data Collection Tools
sec.p: The measures were administered to participants in the same order each time. Prior to obtaining web‐based forms, participants were interviewed remotely to assess their stuttering severity scores. Stuttering severity ratings of adults who stutter were determined with the Stuttering Severity Instrument version 4, which was translated into Turkish by Mutlu et al. (2023; Riley and Bakker 2009). Reliability and validity were evaluated, and very high relative inter‐judge reliability (p < 0.001) and intra‐judge absolute reliability (p < 0.001) were observed. The 10‐min audiovisual recordings were made during a reading assignment and a spontaneous speech test involving an age‐appropriate recognized theme. In order to assess the stuttering severity, digital recordings were examined. Although this instrument classifies stuttering into five categories (i.e., very mild, mild, moderate, severe and very severe), in this study, the stuttering severity of participants was analysed in three groups (i.e., very mild‐mild, moderate and severe‐very severe).

The demographic information of the participants was collected with the demographic information form. The Mindful Attention Awareness Scale (MAAS) was used to collect data to determine their awareness level (Brown and Ryan 2003; Özyeşil et al. 2011). The Ways of Coping with Stress Inventory (WCSI) was used to assess their stress coping styles (Folkman and Lazarus 1985; Şahin and Durak 1995). The Depression Anxiety Stress Scale (DASS) was used to define their depression, anxiety and stress levels (Akın and Çetin 2007; Lovibond and Lovibond 1995).

sec.title: Depression Anxiety Stress Scale (DASS)
sec.p: The Turkish adaptation of the DASS was provided by Akın and Çetin (2007; Lovibond and Lovibond 1995). The authors reported high concurrent validity coefficients of 0.87 and 0.84, respectively, as well as an internal consistency of 0.89 for Cronbach's Alpha (Akın and Çetin 2007). Additionally, the test‐retest and split‐half reliability coefficient scores were 0.99 and 0.96, respectively. The scale is a four‐point Likert scale (0 = not at all appropriate; 3 = completely appropriate). The scale contains 42 items, 14 of which are depression (discontent, helplessness, worthlessness, loss of interest and low energy level); 14 of which are anxiety (the individual's level of situational anxiety, subjective anxiety and muscle response); and 14 of which are stress (difficulty to relax, nervous excitation, easily upsetness, boredom, discomfort, overreaction and intolerance symptoms). The minimum score for each of the three sub‐components is 0, and the maximum score is 42. A high score indicates that the participant's symptoms for that subcomponent have increased. The scale instructs the participant to fill in the scale by considering how appropriate the items are considering the previous week.

sec.title: Mindful Attention Awareness Scale (MAAS)
sec.p: Özyeşil and colleagues (2011) conducted a Turkish adaptation study of the MAAS scale and showed that its Cronbach's Alpha internal consistency was 0.80 and test‐retest correlation was 0.86, which was found to have internal reliability with a coefficient alpha of 0.82 and a test‐retest correlation of 0.81 in Brown and Ryan's (2003) study. The 15‐item scale measures both awareness of immediate experiences and attentiveness. It is a 6‐point Likert scale (1 = almost always, 2 = frequently, 6 = almost never), and the total score indicates awareness (min = 15, max = 90). The higher the score, the higher the awareness level.

sec.title: Ways of Coping With Stress Inventory
sec.p: The Turkish adaptation of the short version of the Ways of Coping with Stress Inventory was prepared by Şahin and Durak (1995; Folkman and Lazarus 1980). The 30‐item scale includes five subscales: self‐confident, optimistic, seeking social support, helpless and submissive approach. Internal consistency (Cronbach's α) for the subscales was as follows: self‐confidence (0.80), optimism (0.68), helplessness (0.73), submissive (0.70) and seeking social support (0.47; Şahin and Durak 1995). Although the seeking social support subscale demonstrated relatively low internal consistency (α = 0.47), the overall scale has been reported as reliable and valid for assessing coping strategies among university students, supported by acceptable reliability coefficients, a distinct factor structure, expected associations of the subscales with related variables, and demonstrated discriminative power (Şahin and Durak 1995). Thus, while the scale is generally reliable, caution is warranted when interpreting the seeking social support subscale scores. Higher scores on self‐confident, optimistic and social support subscales indicate more usage of active coping strategies; higher scores on helpless and submissive subscales indicate more usage of passive coping strategies. The scale is a four‐point Likert type (0 = not at all appropriate; 3 = completely appropriate). Subscale scores are calculated as the mean of the relevant items (range 0−3), with higher scores reflecting more frequent use of the corresponding coping strategy.

sec.title: Data Analysis
sec.p: The mean, standard deviation, median, minimum and maximum values for continuous and discrete variables were provided to display descriptive statistics. Data were evaluated in IBM SPSS Statistics for Windows, Version 26.0 (IBM Corp., released 2019., IBM SPSS Statistics for Windows, Version 26.0., Armonk, NY: IBM Corp.) The suitability of the variables for a normal distribution was evaluated by the Shapiro–Wilk test. The results did not meet the normality assumptions; therefore, nonparametric analysis methods were utilized.

The comparisons of the scales’ scores among three stuttering severity groups (i.e., very mild‐mild, moderate, severe‐very severe) were tested with Kruskal–Wallis. The relationships between the scales’ scores were tested with correlation analysis. The statistical significance level was accepted as 0.05 for all analyses. In significant results of the difference between groups, the Dunn–Bonferroni post‐hoc pairwise comparison test was applied. The results were interpreted according to the adjusted p value.

The Hierarchical Regression Analysis method was used to identify the independent predictors of depression, anxiety and stress scores. The correlations between the independent variables (i.e., mindfulness, active coping styles—self‐confident, optimistic, social support—, and passive coping styles—helpless, submissive) were analysed by Spearman's correlation test, and it was observed that there were no high correlations between the variables that would create multicollinearity. The model fit was assessed using appropriate residual and goodness‐of‐fit statistics, the residuals of the dependent variables (i.e., depression, anxiety, stress) showed a normal distribution. Prior research has indicated that lower depression, anxiety and stress levels have negative significant correlations with higher mindfulness levels and more frequent application of active coping styles and significant positive correlations with more frequent application of passive coping styles (Kaya et al. 2007; Muris et al. 2001; Palmer and Rodger 2009; Weinstein et al. 2009). In this study, there are a number of independent variables (i.e., mindfulness, active coping skills and passive coping styles). In order to determine which variables had the highest statistical predictive power on depression, anxiety and stress levels, independent variables were included in the analysis in three steps. Therefore, in the first step, the mindfulness variable; in the second step, the active coping variables (i.e., self‐confident, optimistic, social support) as a block; and in the third step, the passive coping variables (i.e., helpless, submissive) as a block were added to the analysis.

sec.title: Post‐Hoc Power Analysis
sec.p: Post‐hoc power analyses were performed by using the pwr package with R language (Champely 2020), with a sample size of 47, and (α) = 0.05 significance level; power was calculated as 70% according to the correlation value of −0.355 and 93% according to the correlation value of −0.475. Cohen (1988) defines the size of the correlation coefficient as follows: small effect size: r = 0.10, medium effect size: r = 0.30, and large effect size: r = 0.50. Therefore, it was observed that this study reached a medium effect size. Given the sample size and observed effect sizes, this analysis reflects the possibility that the study could have revealed true associations.

sec.p: Demographic information of participants is shown in Table 1. A Kruskal–Wallis test was conducted to compare the scores of mindfulness, depression, anxiety, stress and subscales of coping with stress styles among stuttering severity groups—very mild‐mild, moderate, severe‐very severe (Table 2). There were no statistically significant differences in the scores of mindfulness, depression, anxiety, stress and subscales of ways of coping with stress among the groups (p > 0.05).

sec.title: Relationships Between Mindfulness, Depression, Anxiety, Stress and Subscales of Ways of Coping With Stress
sec.p: The correlation coefficients of mindfulness, depression, anxiety, stress and subscales of ways of coping with stress and their significance were calculated using the Spearman test (Table 3). There were statistically significant relationships between depression and anxiety (r = 0.724, p < 0.001), depression and stress (r = 0.716, p < 0.001) and anxiety and stress (r = 0.675, p < 0.001) scores. A statistically significant positive relationship between self‐confident and optimistic scores (r = 0.709, p < 0.001) was shown.

sec.title: The Predictive Value of Mindfulness and Coping Styles on Depression, Anxiety and Stress Levels
sec.p: Hierarchical regression analysis was applied to identify the effects of mindfulness, active coping styles and passive coping styles as predictors of depression (Table 4). Model 1 revealed that measures of mindfulness significantly explained 14.8% of the variance in depression score (R2 = 0.148, F = 7.801, p = 0.008). Mindfulness score showed a negative effect on depression (β = −0.28). Self‐confident, optimistic and social support variables did not explain any additional variance and were not significant (R2 = 0.063, F = 1.117, p = 0.353, Model 2). Helpless and submissive variables significantly explained 43.8% of the variance in the depression score (R2 = 0.438, F = 8.066, p = 0.001). Helpless (β = 5.56, p = 0.05) and submissive (β = 6.40, p = 0.07) styles were found to be significant predictors of depression.

caption.p: Hierarchical regression analysis findings of mindfulness and subscales of ways of coping with stress on depression.

sec.p: Hierarchical regression analysis was applied to identify the effects of mindfulness, active coping styles and passive coping styles as predictors of anxiety (Table 5). Model 1 revealed that measures of mindfulness significantly explained 23.5% of the variance in anxiety score (R2 = 0.235, F = 13.824, p = 0.001). Mindfulness score showed a negative effect on anxiety (β = −0.30, p < 0.001). Self‐confident, optimistic and social support variables did not explain any additional variance and were not significant (R2 = 0.010, F = 0.177, p = 0.911, Model 2). Helpless and submissive variables significantly explained 31.4% of the variance in the anxiety score (R2 = 0.559, F = 14.221, p < 0.001). Helpless (β = 5.32, p = 0.01) and submissive (β = 6.38, p = 0.02) styles were found to be significant predictors of anxiety.

sec.p: Hierarchical regression analysis was applied to identify the effects of mindfulness, active coping styles and passive coping styles as predictors of stress (Table 6). Model 1 revealed that measures of mindfulness significantly explained 24.9% of the variance in stress score (R2 = 0.249, F = 14.953, p < 0.001). Mindfulness score showed a negative effect on stress (β = −0.35, p < 0.001). Self‐confident, optimistic and social support variables were added to the model and of these variables only optimistic was found to be significant (β = −7.41, p = 0.01, Model 2). Helpless and submissive variables significantly explained 48.7% of the variance in the stress score (R2 = 0.487, F = 5.135, p = 0.010). Helpless (β = 6.66, p = 0.01) and submissive (β = 0.21, p = 0.95) styles were found to be significant predictors of stress.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This study primarily aimed to examine the predictive value of mindfulness and coping styles on depression, anxiety and stress levels and the relationships between these variables in 47 adults who stutter. Secondarily, the differences in these variables among stuttering severity groups were explored. Findings revealed a significant positive relationship between depression, anxiety and stress levels; mindfulness was found to be a significant predictor of depression, anxiety and stress levels; and helpless and submissive coping styles were found to be significant predictors of depression, and anxiety levels; no significant differences were observed among stuttering severity groups. The findings and clinical implications of this study will be discussed in detail below.

sec.title: Relationships Between Depression, Anxiety, Stress, Mindfulness and Coping Styles
sec.p: As mentioned in the literature review, events that trigger stress and anxiety increase the risk of depression (Mahmoud et al. 2012; Tennant 2002). This study's findings also showed a significant positive relationship between levels of depression, anxiety and stress, which implies that they either increase or decrease together. Although there is not enough data to draw firm conclusions about depressive and stress symptoms, evidence consistently shows that adults who stutter have substantially higher rates of anxiety, with one study reporting a 6‐ to 7‐fold increased risk of meeting criteria for any anxiety disorder compared to age‐ and gender‐matched adults from the general population (Iverach et al. 2009; see, e.g., Kraaimaat et al. 2002; St Clare et al. 2009). The anxiety subscale used in this study was described as a measurement of state anxiety score (Lovibond and Lovibond 1995). This characteristic of the scale makes it a suitable tool to determine the anxiety levels in adults who stutter because prior studies conducted indicated that state anxiety is more common than trait anxiety among adults who stutter (Blumgart et al. 2010; Iverach et al. 2009). Considering the accumulated evidence that adults who stutter have an increased risk of anxiety (e.g., Iverach et al. 2009; Kraaimaat et al. 2002; St Clare et al. 2009), that anxiety is often triggered by situations perceived as stressful, and that stress and anxiety have been shown to be associated with depression levels (Mahmoud et al. 2012; Tennant 2002), it is possible that adults who stutter are more likely to report higher scores of stress and depression alongside anxiety. Longitudinal studies would be useful to further explore the directionality of these relationships.

sec.title: Predictive Effects of Mindfulness and Coping Styles on Depression, Anxiety and Stress
sec.p: The findings of this study revealed that lower levels of mindfulness and higher use of helpless and submissive coping styles (i.e., passive coping styles) were associated with higher reported scores of depression, anxiety and stress. In other words, lower mindfulness levels, along with more frequent use of passive coping styles, were found in this study to be predictors of depression, anxiety and stress. The active coping styles (i.e., self‐confident, optimistic and social support) investigated in this study did not contribute significantly to the model as predictors of depression, anxiety and stress levels. In interpreting these results, it is important to note that the seeking social support subscale demonstrated relatively low internal consistency (α = 0.47). Low reliability increases measurement error and may attenuate true associations; therefore, the non‐significant contribution of the social support subscale to the predictive models should be interpreted with caution, as it may reflect limitations in measurement rather than the absence of an underlying relationship. Thus, the finding that social support seeking did not significantly predict depression, anxiety, or stress levels should not be taken as definitive evidence of the absence of an effect. Previous studies have shown that the risk of anxiety in individuals who stutter is higher than in the general population (e.g., Iverach et al. 2009; Kraaimaat et al. 2002; St Clare et al. 2009). The tendency of depression, anxiety and stress scores to increase together has also been shown in this study and previous studies (Mahmoud et al. 2012; Tennant 2002). Interpretation of these findings raises the question of whether individuals who stutter tend to have lower mindfulness levels and use passive coping strategies more frequently and prevalently compared to the general population.

Comparisons among adults who stutter, grouped by stuttering severity, revealed no significant differences in depression, anxiety, stress levels, mindfulness, or coping styles scores, which is consistent with recent literature on this topic (Blumgart et al. 2012; Manning and Gayle Beck 2013). The overall well‐being of individuals is influenced by the complex interplay of personal, environmental and social factors. These findings, together with previous research, suggest that psychological outcomes in adults who stutter do not appear to stem directly from the observable severity of their stuttering, but instead may arise from broader personal and environmental factors.

sec.title: Clinical Implications
sec.p: Lower mindfulness and greater reliance on passive coping styles have been associated with elevated levels of depression, anxiety and stress, which may consequently have negative individual, social and environmental outcomes. These findings highlight the potential value of incorporating strategies that enhance mindfulness and promote active coping within stuttering interventions. Mindfulness practices may improve individuals’ ability to attend to the present moment, observe experiences nonjudgmentally, and regulate negative thoughts and emotions more adaptively, while fostering functional coping strategies and reducing reliance on dysfunctional approaches can support adaptive stress responses, engagement in daily activities, and social connectedness. Notably, since no significant differences were observed across stuttering severity groups, assessment and intervention when needed targeting mindfulness, and coping mechanisms may be considered for adults who stutter, potentially contributing to improved psychological resilience and overall quality of life. Consistent with these considerations, prior research suggests that mindfulness training can be particularly beneficial for adults who stutter. For example, Israel et al. (2023) found that adults who stutter who practiced mindfulness were better able to approach their experiences with objectivity and self‐compassion, mitigating the negative impact of stuttering on their lives, and emphasized that these skills can be developed through practice. Similarly, Medina et al. (2023) reported that an 8‐week remote mindfulness program led to improvements in quality of life ratings on the Overall Assessment of the Speaker's Experience of Stuttering (OASES; Yaruss and Quesal 2006) for several participants. Collectively, these findings suggest that mindfulness‐based interventions may serve as a valuable complementary approach in stuttering therapy, although further research is warranted to clarify their efficacy and mechanisms of action.

sec.title: Limitations
sec.p: This study has several limitations. The sample size was relatively small, limiting the generalizability of the findings; future research should aim to include larger and more diverse samples to enhance external validity. Cultural factors also warrant consideration, as research in Turkey has shown that the collectivist structure of Turkish culture and the influence of Islam and Sufism on daily life can directly shape coping styles and mindfulness through teachings that emphasize being patient, thankful and trustful (Ahmadi et al. 2018; Ahmadi et al. 2019; Alemdar et al. 2023; Aydın et al. 2025; Cetrez et al. 2020; Kaya and Oskay 2019; Uygur and Beyhan 2024), while family and social support are perceived as a moral responsibility and play a central role in coping styles (Pfundmair et al. 2015; Serbest and Büyükişcan 2012; Toplu‐Demirtaş et al. 2018; Voswinckel et al. 2019). These findings suggest the value of cross‐cultural investigations to examine how sociocultural contexts may shape the observed relationships. In the present study, depression, anxiety and stress were assessed using a single instrument. Future studies could consider multiple measures for each construct to strengthen validity, such as the BDI (Beck et al. 1996) for depression, the Computerized Visual Analog Scale for state anxiety (Abend et al. 2014), and the Perceived Stress Scale (Cohen et al. 1994) for perceived stress. The fixed order of questionnaire administration may also have introduced order effects. Furthermore, prior therapy experiences, including therapy history, content and support group participation, may have influenced responses. Future studies with larger and more diverse samples, alongside longitudinal designs, could help clarify causal relationships and evaluate the impact of interventions over time, providing more robust evidence for clinical practice.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: In conclusion, lower mindfulness levels and more frequent use of passive coping styles appeared to be predictors of higher levels of depression, anxiety and stress. Therefore, mindfulness levels and the frequency of engaging in passive coping strategies appear to be important considerations in decision‐making processes for effectively managing stuttering and its adverse impacts in adults who stutter.
